Doctors sometimes disagree about which medicine is best. But they all agree you shouldn't give a patient poison. It's similar with philosophers: they disagree about many details, but almost all agree that making animals suffer without need is wrong.

It's true, philosophers disagree about almost everything, and you wouldn't conclude from that that anything goes. On the question of animals there's a strong point of convergence: the main ethical theories condemn unnecessary suffering, and it's hard to find anyone who defends factory farming as it exists. So much so that, in a survey of ethics professors in the United States, about 60% rated regularly eating mammal meat as morally bad.
"Do you know any philosopher who defends factory farming as it is today?"
The argument treats every disagreement as a tie. But there are degrees of agreement:
Is causing animals unnecessary suffering wrong?
Does factory farming cause unnecessary suffering on a large scale?
Is killing an animal painlessly wrong?
Do animals have rights in the same sense as humans?
Disagreement on the lower questions doesn't affect the conclusion of the upper ones, which is already enough to condemn almost all the meat that is consumed.
Every field of knowledge has disagreements, and that doesn't make all positions equivalent. Philosophers also disagree about how to ground human rights.

Utilitarianism condemns unnecessary suffering; rights theories condemn using sentient beings as means; virtue ethics condemns cruelty; contractualism, in its recent versions, has been extended to animals. By different routes, they reach similar conclusions.
In a survey of US professors, about 60% of ethics specialists rated regularly eating mammal meat as morally bad, compared with about 20% of professors in other fields.

text.bold: 4. Defenses of factory farming are rare.

paragraph.text: Even philosophers who defend eating meat usually defend only forms very different from current production, such as animals raised with a good life and killed painlessly (B3).

text.bold: 5. The argument usually serves to end the conversation.

paragraph.text: But when you look at what philosophers say about animals, the conclusion is clearer than the phrase suggests.

text.bold: 6. Even on the ideal model there is common ground.

paragraph.text: Among utilitarians, the disagreement about what would come next is real: some defend a plant-only agriculture; Peter Singer grants in theory, but rejects in practice, that raising free-range birds and fish and killing them painlessly might be acceptable; and Steven Davis and George Schedler propose keeping some cattle pasture, a calculation Gaverick Matheny disputed. But, as the political philosopher Alasdair Cochrane notes, all these models condemn the current system: none of them defends intensive farming (Cochrane, 2010, pp. 39–42; see H2).

text.bold: 7. Rival schools each contribute a part.

paragraph.text: Cochrane examines five traditions in political theory, utilitarianism, liberalism, communitarianism, Marxism and care feminism, and points out flaws in all of them. Even so, he concludes that each adds something to what is owed to animals: sentience as the criterion of who counts, the centrality of the individual, the dependence on a social context that supports protection, the lesson that changing the law isn't enough, and the role of emotion in drawing attention to injustice (2010, pp. 136–141). It's one author's reading, and each school has internal critics. But it shows that disagreement between theories doesn't stop them from pointing the same way. Cochrane himself noted in 2010 that the subject was still peripheral in political theory (pp. 145–146); since then it has gained ground, with works such as
(2011), by Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka.

It's true that there is philosophical disagreement about animals, and that it's serious: there are legitimate discussions about the value of animal life, the strength of duties and borderline cases. Recognizing this is a sign of intellectual honesty.
But the disagreement is in the details, not at the center. Almost everyone agrees that unnecessary suffering is wrong, and that's already enough to condemn most of what happens to animals today.
